content: Influenza epidemics typically occur during the winter months in temperate regions and have been responsible for an average of approximately 36,000 deaths annually in the United States during the 1990s. Influenza viruses can also cause pandemics, during which illness and death rates from influenza-related complications increase globally. These viruses affect individuals across all age groups, with the highest infection rates observed among children. However, the rates of severe illness and death are highest among individuals aged over 65 years, children under 2 years, and individuals of any age with medical conditions that increase their risk for influenza-related complications. Vaccination is the primary method for preventing influenza and its severe complications. It is particularly important for healthcare workers and household contacts who frequently interact with high-risk individuals, as they can transmit the virus to these vulnerable populations. Vaccination has been associated with reductions in influenza-related respiratory illness, physician visits, hospitalizations, and deaths among high-risk individuals, as well as reductions in otitis media among children and work absenteeism among adults. Despite substantial increases in vaccination coverage during the 1990s, further improvements are needed, especially among individuals aged over 65 years, children aged 6–23 months, and healthcare workers. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends strategies to improve vaccination rates, such as reminder/recall systems and standing orders programs. While vaccination remains the cornerstone of influenza prevention, antiviral medications are also presented as an adjunct to vaccination. Influenza A and B viruses are the two types responsible for epidemic human disease. Influenza A viruses are further categorized into subtypes based on two surface antigens: hemagglutinin and neuraminidase. Influenza B viruses are not categorized into subtypes. Since 1977, influenza A (H1N1), influenza A (H3N2), and influenza B viruses have been in global circulation. Influenza A (H1N2) viruses, which likely emerged after genetic reassortment between human A (H3N2) and A (H1N1) viruses, began circulating widely in 2001. Both influenza A and B viruses undergo antigenic drift, resulting from point mutations during viral replication. Influenza B viruses undergo antigenic drift less rapidly than influenza A viruses. Immunity to surface antigens, particularly hemagglutinin, reduces the likelihood of infection and disease severity. However, antibody protection is limited to specific virus types or subtypes and may not fully protect against new antigenic variants of the same type or subtype. Influenza viruses are primarily spread from person to person through respiratory droplets from coughing and sneezing. The typical incubation period is 1–4 days, with an average of 2 days. Adults can be infectious from the day before symptom onset to approximately 5 days after illness onset, while children can be infectious for over 10 days. Severely immunocompromised individuals can shed the virus for weeks or months. Common symptoms include fever, myalgia, headache, malaise, nonproductive cough, sore throat, and rhinitis. Among children, otitis media, nausea, and vomiting are also frequently reported. Respiratory illness caused by influenza is difficult to distinguish from illnesses caused by other respiratory pathogens based on symptoms alone. The risks for complications, hospitalizations, and deaths from influenza are higher among individuals aged over 65 years, young children, and individuals with certain underlying health conditions. Estimated rates of influenza-associated hospitalizations vary by age group and epidemic severity. Among children aged 0–4 years, hospitalization rates are highest among those aged 0–1 year and are comparable to rates reported among individuals aged over 65 years. During influenza epidemics from 1979–80 through 2000–01, the estimated number of influenza-associated hospitalizations in the United States ranged from approximately 54,000 to 430,000 per epidemic. An average of approximately 226,000 influenza-related excess hospitalizations occurred annually, with 63% of these hospitalizations occurring among individuals aged over 65 years. Influenza-related deaths can result from pneumonia and exacerbations of cardiopulmonary conditions and other chronic diseases. Deaths among older adults account for over 90% of deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza. In one study of influenza epidemics, approximately 19,000 influenza-associated pulmonary and circulatory deaths occurred per influenza season during 1976–1990, compared with approximately 36,000 deaths during 1990–1999. The number of influenza-associated deaths in the United States may be increasing partly due to the growing number of older individuals. Influenza seasons dominated by influenza A (H3N2) viruses are associated with higher mortality. Vaccination remains the primary option for reducing the impact of influenza in the United States. Both inactivated (killed virus) and live attenuated influenza vaccines are available. The effectiveness of inactivated influenza vaccine depends on the age and immunocompetence of the recipient and the similarity between vaccine and circulating virus strains. Among healthy adults aged under 65 years, the vaccine prevents influenza illness in approximately 70%–90% of cases when vaccine and circulating viruses are antigenically similar. Vaccination also reduces work absenteeism and healthcare resource use. Children aged 6 months and older can develop protective levels of anti-influenza antibodies after vaccination, although the antibody response among high-risk children may be lower than among healthy children. Among older adults, vaccine efficacy in preventing influenza-related hospitalizations or pneumonia ranges from 30%–70%, and the vaccine is 80% effective in preventing influenza-related deaths among nursing home residents. Live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) has demonstrated high efficacy in preventing culture-confirmed influenza among healthy children and adults. In randomized controlled trials, LAIV has shown efficacy rates of over 90% in preventing influenza during well-matched seasons. LAIV has also been associated with reductions in febrile otitis media and febrile illnesses. Influenza vaccination is cost-effective, reducing both healthcare costs and productivity losses.
